title: Book 1, Chapter 3 — Congress of the Peloponnesian Confederacy at Lacedaemon
paragraphs: The Athenians and Peloponnesians already had these grounds of complaint against each other. Corinth complained that Potidæa, her colony, was under siege, with Corinthian and Peloponnesian citizens inside it. Athens complained that the Peloponnesians had incited to revolt a town of hers, a member of her alliance and a contributor to her revenue, and had come and were openly fighting against her on the side of the Potidæans. Even so, war had not yet broken out. The truce still held for the time being, since Corinth was acting on her own account.

But the siege of Potidæa ended her inaction, for she had men inside it and feared for the place. She at once summoned the allies to Lacedaemon, came there herself, and loudly accused Athens of breaking the treaty and of wronging the Peloponnese. The Aeginetans, who from fear of Athens sent no formal representation, came with her, and in secret proved among the most urgent advocates for war, claiming that they did not have the independence the treaty guaranteed them. The Lacedaemonians then sent word to any other allies and to anyone else who had complaints of Athenian aggression, held their regular assembly, and invited them to speak. Many came forward and made their separate accusations. Among them the Megarians, in a long list of grievances, drew special attention to their exclusion from the ports of the Athenian empire and from the market of Athens, in defiance of the treaty. Last of all the Corinthians came forward. They had let the others inflame the Lacedaemonians first, and now followed with a speech to this effect:

“Lacedaemonians, you trust your own constitution and social order, and that trust makes you receive any remarks of ours about other powers with some skepticism. This is the source of your moderation, but also of the rather limited knowledge you show in dealing with foreign politics. Time after time we raised our voice to warn you of the blows Athens was about to deal us. Time after time, instead of taking the trouble to judge the worth of what we told you, you were content to suspect the speakers of acting from private interest. So you did not call these allies together before the blow fell. You have put it off until we are smarting under it. Among these allies we have as good a title as any to speak, since we have the greatest complaints to make, of Athenian outrage and of Lacedaemonian neglect. Now if these assaults on the rights of Hellas had been made in the dark, you might not know the facts, and it would be our duty to enlighten you. As it is, long speeches are not needed. You see servitude accomplished for some of us and planned for others, in particular for our allies, and you see the aggressor making long preparations against the hour of war. Or what, pray, is the meaning of their taking Corcyra by fraud and holding it against us by force? What of the siege of Potidæa? One of these places lies most conveniently for any action against the Thracian towns, while the other would have contributed a very large navy to the Peloponnesians?

“You are responsible for all this. It was you who first let them fortify their city after the Median war, and later build the long walls. Then and now you keep depriving of freedom not only the peoples they have enslaved but even your own allies up to now. The true author of a people’s subjugation is not so much the one who carries it out as the power that could prevent it and permits it, above all when that power claims the glory of being the liberator of Hellas. At last we are gathered here, though gathering was not easy, and even now our aims are not settled. We should no longer be asking whether we have been wronged. We should be asking how to defend ourselves. The aggressors have matured plans, and against our indecision they have put aside threats and moved to action. We know the paths along which Athenian aggression travels, and how insidiously it advances. She may take some confidence from thinking that your dullness of perception keeps you from noticing her. But that is nothing beside the impulse she will gain from knowing that you do see, and do not care to interfere. You, Lacedaemonians, alone of all the Hellenes, do nothing. You defend yourselves not by acting but by seeming about to act. You alone wait until an enemy’s power has doubled, when you could have crushed it in its infancy. Yet you had a name for being dependable; in your case, we fear, that name said more than the truth. As we ourselves know, the Mede had time to come from the ends of the earth to Peloponnese, and no force of yours worth mentioning went out to meet him. But he was a distant enemy. Athens at least is a near neighbor, and still you utterly ignore her. Against Athens you choose defense over attack, and you leave the outcome to chance by postponing the struggle until she is far stronger than she was. And you know that, on the whole, the rock on which the barbarian was wrecked was himself, and that if Athens, our present enemy, has not many times destroyed us, we owe that more to her blunders than to your protection. Indeed, hopes placed in you have before now ruined some, whose faith made them neglect to prepare.

“We hope none of you will take this remonstrance as hostility. Men remonstrate with friends who are mistaken; accusations they keep for enemies who have wronged them. Besides, we think we have as good a right as anyone to point out a neighbor’s faults, particularly in view of the great contrast between the two national characters. As far as we can tell, you hardly perceive this contrast. You have never yet considered what kind of opponents the Athenians will be, or how widely and completely they differ from you. The Athenians are addicted to innovation, and quick both in forming a design and in carrying it out. You have a genius for keeping what you have, and you have no inventiveness whatever; when forced to act, you never go far enough. They are adventurous beyond their power and daring beyond their judgment, and they stay hopeful in danger. You attempt less than your power allows, distrust even what your judgment approves, and think there is no escape from danger. They act promptly where you put things off. They are always abroad, and you never leave home. They hope that being away will add to their gains; you fear that advancing will put at risk what you left behind. They press a success quickly, and they are slow to fall back from a reverse. They spend their bodies freely for their country; their intellect they keep jealously for her service. A plan left unexecuted is to them a real loss, and a successful enterprise something of a failure. If an undertaking fails, fresh hopes soon make up the lack. They alone can call a thing hoped for a thing gained, because they act on their resolutions so fast. So they labor on through trouble and danger all their lives, with little chance to enjoy anything, always occupied in getting. Their idea of a holiday is to do what the moment requires, and hard work seems to them less of a misfortune than the peace of a quiet life. In a word, one might truly say that they were born to take no rest themselves and to allow none to others.

“That is Athens, your antagonist. And still, Lacedaemonians, you delay. You do not see that peace lasts longest for those who take as much care to show they will not submit to injustice as to use their power justly. Your notion of fair dealing is quite different. You hold that by doing no harm to others you avoid having to risk your own fortunes to stop others from harming you. You could hardly have succeeded with such a policy even beside a neighbor like yourselves. As we have just shown, against Athens your ways are out of date. In politics, as in the arts, new methods always win out. Fixed customs serve best for communities left in peace, but those under constant necessity of action need constantly improved methods. That is why Athens, with her vast experience, has gone further than you along the road of innovation.

“Let your delay end here, at least. Help your allies now, and Potidæa above all, as you promised, by invading Attica quickly. Do not hand friends and kindred over to their bitterest enemies, and so drive the rest of us in despair to another alliance. Neither the Gods who received our oaths nor the men who witnessed them would condemn that step. When desertion forces a people to seek new ties, the broken treaty is not their fault but the fault of the power that fails to help its confederate. If you will only act, we will stand by you. It would be unnatural for us to change, and we should never find so congenial an ally. For these reasons, choose the right course, and take care that Peloponnese under your supremacy does not fall short of the prestige it held under your ancestors.”

Such were the words of the Corinthians. Athenian envoys happened to be at Lacedaemon on other business. When they heard the speeches, they felt they ought to appear before the Lacedaemonians. They did not mean to defend themselves against the charges the cities were bringing. They meant to show, taking the whole situation into view, that the matter should not be decided in haste but needed more consideration. They also wished to point out the great power of Athens, to remind the old of what they knew and inform the young of what they did not, thinking their words might lead the Lacedaemonians to prefer tranquility to war. So they approached the Lacedaemonians and said that, if there was no objection, they too wished to address the assembly. The Lacedaemonians told them to come forward. The Athenians stepped up and spoke as follows:

“We did not come here to argue with your allies. We came on the business our state sent us to attend to. But the vehemence of the outcry against us has persuaded us to speak. We will not answer the accusations of the cities (you are not, in any case, the judges before whom we or they can plead). We want to keep you from taking the wrong course on weighty matters by giving in too readily to your allies’ persuasion. We also want to show, by going over the whole indictment, that we hold our possessions by a fair title and that our country deserves consideration. We need not go back to remote antiquity, where we could cite tradition but not what our hearers have seen. But we must refer to the Median War and to recent history, though we are rather tired of raising the subject again and again. In that war we took great risks to gain certain advantages. You shared in the solid results, so do not try to deny us every share in whatever good the glory may do us. Still, we tell the story not so much to deprecate hostility as to bear witness against it, and to show what sort of antagonist Athens is likely to prove, if you are so ill advised as to go to war with her. We say that at Marathon we stood in the front line and faced the barbarian alone. When he came a second time and we could not match him on land, we embarked on our ships with our whole people and fought at Salamis. That kept him from taking the Peloponnesian states one at a time and ravaging them with his fleet, since the number of his vessels would have made any joint defense impossible. The invader himself gave the best proof of this. Beaten at sea, he judged his power no longer what it had been, and withdrew as fast as he could with most of his army.

“That, then, was the outcome, and it was clearly shown that the cause of Hellas rested on her fleet. We supplied three very valuable things toward that outcome: the most ships, the ablest commander, and the most unhesitating patriotism. Our ships numbered little less than two-thirds of the four hundred in all. Our commander was Themistocles, who above all brought about the battle in the straits, universally acknowledged to have saved our cause. This is in fact why you honored him as you never honored any foreign visitor. In daring patriotism we had no rivals. No reinforcements came from behind us, and everything ahead of us was already conquered. Even so, we had the spirit to leave our city and give up our property (rather than desert the rest of the league or scatter and deprive them of our help), and to throw ourselves into our ships and face the danger, without a thought of resenting your failure to help us. We maintain, therefore, that we gave you as much as we received. You had something to fight for: the cities you had left were still full of your homes, and you could hope to enjoy them again. Your coming was prompted as much by fear for yourselves as for us. At any rate, you never appeared until we had nothing left to lose. We left behind a city that was no longer a city, and risked our lives for a city that existed only in desperate hope. So we took our full share in your deliverance and our own. If we had followed others, and let fear for our land make us side with the Mede before you came, or if our ruin had broken our spirit and kept us from boarding our ships, you would have been too weak at sea to fight, and he would have gained his ends without a struggle.

“Surely, Lacedaemonians, neither the patriotism we showed in that crisis nor the wisdom of our counsels earns us our extreme unpopularity with the Hellenes, at least not for our empire. We did not win that empire by violence. You were unwilling to see the war against the barbarian through to the end, and the allies came over to us and asked us themselves to take the command. Then the nature of the case forced us to build our empire up to its present height, fear being our chief motive, with honor and interest following. And in the end, when nearly everyone hated us, when some had already revolted and been put down, and when you were no longer the friends you had been but objects of suspicion and dislike, it no longer seemed safe to give up our empire, especially since all who left us would go over to you. And no one can blame a people for making the best provision it can for its interest when the risks are tremendous.

“You, Lacedaemonians, at any rate, have used your supremacy to settle the states of Peloponnese in the way that suits you. If at the time we speak of you had stayed with the matter to the end, and had become hated in command, we are sure you would have been just as galling to the allies, and would have had to choose between firm government and danger to yourselves. It follows that we did nothing very remarkable, or contrary to the common practice of mankind, when we accepted an empire that was offered to us and then refused to give it up. Three of the strongest motives, fear, honor and interest, forced us. Nor were we the first to set this example, for it has always been the rule that the weaker is subject to the stronger. Besides, we thought ourselves worthy of our position, and so did you until now, when calculations of interest have made you raise the cry of justice. No one has ever yet put justice forward to stop his own ambition when he had a chance to gain something by force. All praise is due to those who, though not so far above human nature as to refuse dominion, still respect justice more than their position requires.

“We think our moderation would be best shown if others stood in our place. Yet even our fairness has brought us, most unreasonably, condemnation instead of approval. We have waived some of our rights in contract suits with our allies and let impartial laws at Athens decide them, and for this we have the name of being litigious. No one asks why other imperial powers are not reproached in this way, though they treat their subjects less moderately than we do. The secret is that where force can be used, there is no need of law. But our subjects are so accustomed to dealing with us as equals that they resent every defeat that goes against their notions of justice, whether it comes from a legal judgment or from the power our empire gives us. They forget to be grateful that they keep most of their possessions, and they are angrier at the loss of a part than if we had set law aside from the start and openly indulged our covetousness. Had we done that, not even they would have denied that the weaker must yield to the stronger. Men, it seems, are angrier at legal wrong than at violent wrong. The first looks like being cheated by an equal, the second like being compelled by a superior. At any rate they endured much worse treatment from the Mede, yet they find our rule severe. That is to be expected, for the present always weighs heavily on the conquered. One thing at least is certain. If you overthrew us and took our place, you would soon lose the goodwill that fear of us has won you, if your policy today is anything like the sample you gave during your short command against the Mede. Your life at home is governed by rules and institutions that cannot agree with those of others, and abroad your citizens follow neither those rules nor the ones the rest of Hellas recognizes.

“Take time, then, to form your resolution, for the matter is a great one. Do not let the opinions and complaints of others persuade you to bring trouble on yourselves. Consider, before you are in it, how much accident counts in war. As a war goes on, it usually turns into a matter of chances, and neither of us is exempt from them; we must risk the outcome blindly. It is a common mistake in going to war to start at the wrong end, to act first and to discuss the matter only after disaster has come. But we are not yet so misguided, and, as far as we can see, neither are you. So while both of us can still choose rightly, we bid you not to dissolve the treaty or break your oaths, but to settle our differences by arbitration, as our agreement provides. If you refuse, we call to witness the gods who heard the oaths. If you begin hostilities, we will try, whatever course you take, not to be slow in repelling you.”

Such were the words of the Athenians. When the Lacedaemonians had heard the allies’ complaints against the Athenians and the Athenians’ remarks in reply, they had everyone leave and discussed the question among themselves. The majority all reached the same conclusion: the Athenians were plainly the aggressors, and war must be declared at once. But Archidamus, the Lacedaemonian king, who had a reputation as a wise and moderate man, stepped forward and made this speech:

“Lacedaemonians, I have lived long enough to have seen many wars. I see men of my own age among you, who will not fall into the common misfortune of longing for war out of inexperience or out of a belief that it is advantageous and safe. If we look at it soberly, the war you are debating now would be one of the greatest magnitude. In a struggle with Peloponnesians and neighbors, our strength is of the same kind, and we can move swiftly to any point. But think of a struggle with a people who live far away, who are extraordinarily familiar with the sea, and who are in the highest state of preparation in every other respect. They have wealth, private and public, ships, horses, heavy infantry, and a population such as no other Hellenic place can match, and besides all this a number of tributary allies. What justifies us in rashly beginning such a struggle? What do we trust in, that we rush into it unprepared? Our ships? There we are inferior, and if we are to train and become their match, time must pass. Our money? There we are far worse off. We have none in our treasury, and we are not ready to contribute it from private funds. We might perhaps feel confident in our superiority in heavy infantry and numbers, which will allow us to invade and devastate their lands. But the Athenians have plenty of other land in their empire, and can import what they need by sea. And if we try to stir up their allies to revolt, we shall have to support them with a fleet, since most of them are islanders. What, then, is our war to be? Unless we can beat them at sea, or cut them off from the revenues that feed their navy, we shall meet with little but disaster. Meanwhile our honor will be committed to going on, especially if people think we began the quarrel. Let us never be lifted up by the fatal hope that devastating their lands will end the war quickly. I fear rather that we may leave it as a legacy to our children, so unlikely is it that the Athenian spirit will be enslaved by its land, or Athenian experience cowed by war.

“I am not telling you to be so unfeeling as to let them injure your allies, or to refrain from exposing their intrigues. I am telling you not to take up arms at once. Send to them and remonstrate, in a tone neither too much like war nor too much like submission, and use the interval to complete our own preparations. We shall do this, first, by gaining allies, Hellenic or barbarian, it does not matter, provided they add to our strength in ships or in money — I say Hellenic or barbarian because the law of self-preservation removes any odium from such an addition, for all who, like us, are the targets of Athenian designs — and second, by developing our own resources. If they listen to our embassy, so much the better. If not, in two or three years our position will be considerably stronger, and we can attack them then, if we think fit. Perhaps by then the sight of our preparations, backed by language just as meaningful, will have inclined them to submit, while their land is still untouched and their counsels can still aim at keeping advantages not yet lost. You should regard their land only as a hostage in your hands, and the better it is cultivated, the more valuable a hostage. You ought to spare it as long as possible, and not make them desperate, which would make them harder to deal with. If, while we are unprepared, the complaints of our allies hurry us into laying it waste, beware that we do not bring deep disgrace and deep perplexity upon Peloponnese. Complaints, whether of communities or of individuals, can be settled. But a war undertaken by a coalition for the separate interests of its members, with a course no one can foresee, does not easily end in a creditable settlement.

“And no one need think it cowardice that a number of confederates hesitate before attacking a single city. The Athenians have allies as numerous as ours, and allies that pay tribute. War depends less on arms than on money, which makes arms useful, and this is truer than ever in a struggle between a land power and a sea power. So let us first provide money, and not be swept along by our allies’ talk before we have done so. We shall carry the largest share of responsibility for the consequences, good or bad, and therefore we also have the right to examine them calmly.

“As for the slowness and delay that they criticize most in us, you need not blush for them. If we go to war unprepared, we shall only delay its end by hurrying its beginning. Besides, ours has always been a free and famous city. What they condemn is really only a wise moderation. Because of it, we alone are not insolent in success, and we give way less than others in misfortune. We are not carried away by the pleasure of being cheered on to risks our judgment condemns, and when we are provoked, accusations meant to exasperate us do not persuade us any the more. We are both warlike and wise, and our sense of order makes us so. We are warlike because self-control has honor as a chief constituent, and honor has bravery. We are wise because we are brought up with too little learning to despise the laws and with too strict a self-control to disobey them. We are raised not to be too knowing in useless matters — such as the knowledge that can criticize an enemy’s plans plausibly in theory but cannot attack them with equal success in practice — and we are taught that our enemies’ schemes are much like our own, and that the freaks of chance cannot be settled by calculation. In practice we always prepare against an enemy on the assumption that his plans are good. Indeed, we should rest our hopes not on his blunders but on the soundness of our own provisions. And we should not suppose that one man differs much from another, but think that the advantage goes to the one reared in the strictest school. These practices, which our ancestors passed on to us and which have always profited us, must not be abandoned. We must not be hurried into deciding in one short day a question that concerns many lives, fortunes and cities, and in which honor is deeply involved. We must decide calmly, and our strength gives us a special ability to do so. As for the Athenians, send to them about Potidæa, send about the allies’ alleged wrongs, especially as they are ready to give legal satisfaction. Law forbids proceeding against one who offers arbitration as if he were a wrongdoer. Meanwhile do not neglect to prepare for war. This decision will be the best for yourselves and the most terrible for your opponents.”
That was the speech of Archidamus. Last to come forward was Sthenelaidas, one of the ephors for that year, who spoke to the Lacedaemonians as follows:

“I do not pretend to understand the long speech of the Athenians. They said a good deal in praise of themselves, but nowhere denied that they are injuring our allies and Peloponnese. And yet if they behaved well against the Mede then, but ill toward us now, they deserve double punishment for having ceased to be good and for having become bad. We meanwhile are the same then and now. If we are wise, we shall not disregard the wrongs of our allies, or put off until tomorrow the duty of assisting those who must suffer today. Others have much money and ships and horses, but we have good allies, whom we must not give up to the Athenians. Nor must we decide the matter by lawsuits and words, since it is anything but in word that we are harmed; we must render instant and powerful help. And let us not be told that it is fitting for us to deliberate while under injustice. Long deliberation is rather fitting for those who have injustice in contemplation. Vote therefore, Lacedaemonians, for war, as the honor of Sparta demands. Neither allow the further aggrandizement of Athens, nor betray our allies to ruin, but with the gods let us advance against the aggressors.”

With these words he, as ephor, himself put the question to the assembly of the Lacedaemonians. He said that he could not determine which was the loudest acclamation (their mode of decision is by acclamation, not by voting). In fact he wished to make them declare their opinion openly and so increase their ardor for war. Accordingly he said: “All Lacedaemonians who are of opinion that the treaty has been broken and that Athens is guilty, leave your seats and go there,” pointing out a certain place; “all who are of the opposite opinion, there.” They stood up accordingly and divided, and those who held that the treaty had been broken were in a decided majority. The Lacedaemonians then summoned the allies and told them that their opinion was that Athens had been guilty of injustice, but that they wished to convoke all the allies and put it to the vote, so that they might make war, if they decided to do so, on a common resolution. Having thus gained their point, the delegates returned home at once, and the Athenian envoys a little later, when they had dispatched the objects of their mission. This decision of the assembly, that the treaty had been broken, was made in the fourteenth year of the thirty years’ truce, which was entered into after the affair of Euboea.

The Lacedaemonians voted that the treaty had been broken and that the war must be declared. They did so not so much because they were persuaded by the arguments of the allies as because they feared the growth of the power of the Athenians, seeing most of Hellas already subject to them.
